## Stein operators

For an operator $\mathcal{A}_{x}$ to be a Stein operator for a target distribution $p(x)$, it must satisfy the following key property:

$$
\mathbb{E}_{X\sim p}[\mathcal{A}_{X} f(X)] = 0.
$${#eq-stein-op}

For $\mathcal{F}$ which include a non-trivial linear subspace, we can see that $\mathcal{A}_{x}$ must be linear, because expectation is linear.

<!-- A commented-out paragraph, written for this fixture, standing in for the
two draft asides the source post carries: the segmenter must protect it under
the livingthing configuration and ignore it under stylebot's. -->

A popular choice is to set the Stein Operator to
$$
\mathcal{A}_{x} f(x):=f(x)  \nabla_x \cdot \log p(x)+\nabla_x \cdot f(x).
$${#eq-langevin-stein-op}

## Stein discrepancy

We make @eq-stein-op into a quantity that depends on two, potentially-_different_ densities by taking the expectation over a different density $q$:

$$
\mathbb{E}_{x\sim q}[\mathcal{A}_{x} f(X)]=0
$$ {#eq-inner-stein-disc}

Spoiler: it turns out that this _does_ do something useful.
Thus
$$\begin{aligned}
S(q, p)
&=\left\|\beta_{q, p}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}^d}^2\\
&=\mathbb{E}_{x, x' \sim q}\left[\kappa_p\left(x, x'\right)\right]
\end{aligned}$$
where

$$
S(p, q)=\mathbb{E}_{x, x' \sim p}\left[\boldsymbol{\delta}_{q, p}(x)^{\top} k\left(x, x'\right) \boldsymbol{\delta}_{q, p}\left(x'\right)\right], $$ where $\boldsymbol{\delta}_{q, p}(x)=s_q(x)-s_p(x)$ is the score difference between $p$ and $q$.

It _is_ a mess to write out in full though.

```python
def stein_kernel(k, score_p):
    """The Steinalized kernel, for the record."""
    return k
```
